#9392. Why Kids with ADHD Get Stuck in the Screen-Time Loop. And How to Break It.

The adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games. Learn why ADHD brains get hooked on these “other stimulants,” and how to protect them.

Screen addiction is not the problem. Your child is not hooked on their phone, but rather the endless loop of novelty, stimulation, and unpredictable rewards streaming through it. It’s the dopamine; not the device.

Once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one. Here’s the central point: Phones and video games weren’t as addictive before they got connected to the Internet. A standalone game that you can beat has an ending. A connected game like Fortnite, Roblox, or Minecraft never ends.

For a kid with ADHD, whose brain runs on a dopamine deficit, the Internet is impossible to resist – by design. We hand the most addictive delivery system ever built to the most vulnerable brains, and then ask them to show self-control. That’s not a fair fight.

Adolescents and teens with ADHD find screens irresistible, and it’s no wonder why. The ADHD brain is dopamine-deficient, and screens deliver dopamine instantly, reliably, and without effort. Almost everything else in life – school, sports, chores, homework – delivers dopamine slowly, inconsistently, and with lots of effort. The brain always chooses the path of least resistance to its dopamine.

This isn’t a character flaw or a discipline problem. It’s neurology. The dopamine hit from a connected screen is more powerful and more reinforcing for an ADHD brain than it is for a neurotypical one because the ADHD brain is always hunting for dopamine.

[Download: Managing and Safeguarding Your Child’s Screen Time]

A 2023 meta-analysis of more than 81,000 children found that two or more hours a day of screen time were associated with significantly elevated ADHD risk compared with less than two hours.1 Large longitudinal data from a separate study, which tracked more than 10,000 kids for two years, found that more screen time predicted increased ADHD – and that changes in brain structure helped explain the link.2

Imaging research has tied greater screen time to altered development in the orbitofrontal cortex, lateral prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex – the regions that govern attention, cognitive control, and reward.

Back in the 1950s, the psychologist B.F. Skinner discovered something the entire tech industry would later weaponize: The most powerful way to drive a behavior isn’t to reward it every time, but to reward it unpredictably. It’s called a variable-ratio reinforcement schedule, and it’s the most addictive reward pattern known to behavioral science.

It is why slot machines are built as they are. You pull the lever, and you might get nothing, or you might hit the jackpot. Not knowing is what keeps you pulling.

[Read: How Can I Help My Teen Better Manage Screen Time?]

The same mechanism is now built into the games and apps your child uses every day. The loot box that might contain something rare. The next Roblox round that might go better. The Snapchat notification that might be from someone who matters. The Fortnite match that might end in a Victory Royale. The brain releases dopamine in anticipation of the reward, not when it arrives. This is why your child can’t stop.

But disconnect the device, and the compulsion largely collapses: the variable rewards stop, the social pressure disappears, and the relentless loop finally ends. You don’t have to eliminate every screen, but you must control the connection.

The brain’s prefrontal cortex (the executive function center) isn’t fully developed until around age 25, and perhaps later in an individual with ADHD. Every year you delay access to the Internet is another year of maturity for your child’s executive function system before it’s asked to regulate the most dysregulating product ever made.

This is why a growing chorus of researchers is now urging parents to delay smartphones until at least high school (around age 14) and social media until at least age 16. The logic is simple: Let the most vulnerable period of brain development happen before your child can access the loop.

Here’s the empowering part: You control the devices, the accounts, the passwords, the router, and the timing of introduction. The strategy below is about exerting that control through environmental design – not nagging, not negotiating, not hoping a dysregulated brain suddenly regulates itself.

STEP 1: Make a pact. Counter the “I’m the only one without a phone” argument by encouraging three or four other families to agree to delay access together. Ask the parents of your child’s friends to make the pact. It’s easier to hold the line together than alone.

STEP 2: Stop competing with the screen. Control access to the dopamine source through environmental design, not willpower. Screens go in a central location after a certain hour. Devices charge outside bedrooms, every night, no exceptions.

STEP 3: Build “earn-access” systems. Screens become available only after the non-negotiables are done. Homework must be completed, then Xbox. Follow the simple, consistent rules every single day. The structure does the work so you don’t have to issue the reminder.

Michael McLeod is the founder of GrowNOW ADHD and the author of The Executive Function Playbook.

#9390. Psychiatry ICD-10 Codes

This is a comprehensive table of psychiatry ICD 10 codes used by researchers and healthcare professionals and personnel – nurses, medical coders, physicians, et al. This table has been curated for psychiatrists and mental health specialists to include all psychiatry ICD 10 codes and classifications relevant to psychiatric and mental health conditions.

The World Health Organization originally authorized the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) for mortality coding and classification from United States death certificates. A Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) was developed for medical diagnoses, and a Procedure Coding System (ICD-10-PCS) was used to classify inpatient procedures. Psychiatry ICD-10 codes in the ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS replace and update psychiatry ICD codes in all three volumes of the ICD-9-CM.

#9389. The ADHD Friendship Recipe

Here’s how to stir up stronger connections, repair misunderstandings, and nurture relationships.

Time, similarities, vibes, and luck – these are the four core ingredients of friendship. Blended into the mix for adults with ADHD are anxiety, rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD), impulsivity, and social acuity.

The friendship recipe varies by person and circumstance, but the following strategies almost always help.

The challenge: Attention regulation problems may cause you to mentally drift, dominate conversations, or impulsively interrupt.

[Get This Free Download: The ADHD Friendship Guide for Adults]

You’re tracking multiple stimuli simultaneously – body language, tone, word choice, environmental distractions – while managing your own impulses. This requires significantly more energy than most people realize and can result in unintentional social withdrawal.

Use this gauge to monitor your energy levels throughout a social interaction: 10 = Fully charged 4 = Running low; time to recharge 0 = Want to hide under the covers

You may fear that recharging will damage your relationships, but taking time to rest is the smart choice that allows you to show up as your best self in your relationships.

The dopamine thrill of a new friendship can cause us to text too frequently, share too much too soon, or pressure still-developing friendships. Avoid coming on too strong.

[Read: ADHD and the Social Processing Gap]

Sometimes the challenge isn’t making friends but discerning whether a particular person deserves space in your life.

People pleasing, over-apologizing, overthinking, and shame spirals are signs of RSD.

Amy Kempe, LPC, is the owner of Authentic Life Therapy in Philadelphia.

#9388. What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”

Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

is the Poler Family Professor of Psychology at Amherst College. Her latest trade book, published in North America as Why We Act: Turning Bystanders Into Moral Rebels (Harvard University Press) and internationally as The Bystander Effect: The Psychology of Courage and Inaction (HarperCollins), examines why good people so often stay silent or do nothing in the face of wrongdoing.

#9386. ADHD Medications May Improve Brain Fog in Perimenopausal Women: New Research

Preliminary evidence shows self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.

Stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego. (These findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.)1

During the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD? Executive Dysfunction in Perimenopause: A Scoping Review of the Role of ADHD Medications,” researchers discussed the effectiveness of two ADHD medications: lisdexamphetamine (brand name: Vyvanse), a stimulant, and atomoxetine, a non-stimulant. They studied the impact of these medications on cognition and ADHD symptom severity in women aged 45 to 60 years during the perimenopausal period. The systematic review included three crossover randomized controlled trials involving 60 patients and two cross-sectional studies of 6,048 patients from Iceland and the U.K.

The study found that both lisdexamphetamine (LDX) and atomoxetine (ATX) significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction, as measured by the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, compared to placebo. The BADDS scores for LDX users dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared to 29.8 with placebo. The BADDS scores for ATX users fell from 38.6 to 25.5, compared to 30.1 with placebo. Neuroimaging data from a subset of women taking LDX further supports these findings.

During perimenopause, declining or fluctuating estrogen levels affect dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. As a result, many perimenopausal women experience “brain fog,” which is an umbrella term for forgetfulness, slow thinking, difficulty finding words, and reduced concentration, which can also be a symptom of ADHD. This overlap often leaves clinicians trying to discern whether a patient’s brain fog stems from hormonal fluctuations or undiagnosed ADHD, or both.

“Many women at perimenopause notice changes in focus, memory, and organization that look a lot like ADHD, and the two can be hard to tell apart,” said lead author Jennifer Tat, M.D. candidate and fourth-year medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

In an ADDitude survey of more than 5,000 women with diagnosed and undiagnosed ADHD, 94% of survey respondents said their ADHD symptoms grew more severe during perimenopause and menopause. During this stage, respondents said the most impactful ADHD symptoms were brain fog or memory issues, and overwhelm, both of which 70% of women said had a “life-altering impact” in their 40s and 50s.

“Brain fog became unmanageable,” wrote one 45-year-old mother of two who entered perimenopause at age 41. “Distractibility increased and my inability to complete work tasks in an appropriate amount of time decreased. I began spending all night working just to keep up. Things that I used to have unconscious strategies to deal with were no longer manageable.”

“I never experienced rage or brain fog before perimenopause,” wrote one woman. “Overwhelm has been more frequent in recent years, and depression began in my 40s. I definitely attribute some of this to hormonal changes.”

“In perimenopause, the brain fog and memory, inattention, distractibility, perfectionism, hyperactivity, and restlessness issues become progressively worse,” wrote a 52-year-old woman diagnosed with ADHD at age 50. “I have always had these symptoms, but I was able to manage them with systems that I created for myself. My ability to manage them has declined significantly, and this makes these symptoms seem like they are the worst they have ever been.”

While preliminary evidence from the systematic review found ADHD medications improve subjective executive function, the medications had little to no significant impact on objective cognitive measures, according to tests measuring working memory and sustained attention.

In the ADDitude article “Could ADHD Medications Improve Memory, Focus & Organization in Menopausal Women? The Research Says Yes,” the late Thomas E. Brown, Ph.D., described how his research with C. Neill Epperson, M.D., found ADHD medications alleviated cognitive problems resembling ADHD symptoms in menopausal women without ADHD

The series of three studies measured symptoms with BADDS, which Brown developed. The first study found that ATX treatment significantly improved BADDS scores for working memory; focus scores improved in BADDS scores for women treated with ATX.2 In the second study, executive functions improved, including an objective measure of short-term working memory, in 41% of menopausal women taking 20 to 60 mg LDX daily, compared to 17% for the women on the placebo.3 The third study examined the effects of LDX on the brain functioning of women with no history of ADHD, but with reported cognitive difficulties with working memory, organization, focus, and attention that had begun during menopause.4

“As predicted, neuroimaging data showed that LDX activated executive networks in specific areas of the brain,” Brown wrote. “Those data also showed that LDX’s effect on specific brain regions was associated with improved BADDS scores overall, and with BADDS scores for activation and alertness/effort. Imaging data indicated that improvements in brain activation were significantly larger when women were on LDX than when they were on placebo.”

The studies were published in peer-reviewed medical journals in 2011, 2015, and 2017; however, Brown wrote in 2021, “results of that research have not yet been widely recognized.”

There is currently no FDA-approved pharmacological intervention for executive dysfunction and brain fog during perimenopause or menopause. Research on the most effective treatments for ADHD during perimenopause is limited as well. That said, Patricia Quinn, M.D., explained during a 2026 ADDitude webinar that available data and observational evidence suggest that many women could benefit from estrogen supplementation and increased stimulant dosages during this phase.

“Perimenopause is when you need the most help, the most support,” Quinn said in her webinar, “Perimenopause in Women with ADHD.” “Estrogen… makes your stimulant more effective.”

One roadblock to care is the fact that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate menopause, according to a study published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health. The 2026 study cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”5

Combined, these preliminary findings could open the door to a nonhormone therapeutic option for addressing perimenopausal executive dysfunction, according to researcher Tat.

“Our review found early signs that ADHD medications may help women feel more on top of their daily lives,” Tat said. “While it’s too early to recommend these medications, a quick screen for ADHD symptoms is a simple step that could help women get the right care.”

2Epperson, C.N., Pittman, B., Czarkowski, K.A., Bradley, J., Quinlan, D.M., & Brown, T.E. (2011). Impact of atomoxetine on subjective attention and memory difficulties in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. Menopause. https://doi.org/10.1097/gme.0b013e3181fcafd6

3Epperson, C.N., Shanmugan, S., Kim, D.R., Mathews, S., Czarkowski, K.A., Bradley, J., Appleby, D.H., Iannelli, C., Sammel, M.D., & Brown, T.E. (2015). The link was modest overall but stronger among girls and among teenagers.

Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

#9384. Non-Stimulant ADHD Treatment Options: What to Know

Exploring non-stimulant ADHD treatment? Use these questions to guide your next doctor discussion.

Navigating Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) treatment options as an adult can feel overwhelming, but finding a treatment plan that aligns with your specific health goals is an important first step. ADHD treatment isn’t one-size-fits-all. Non-stimulant treatments offer an option without controlled-substance management.

Finding a treatment is a collaborative process. My role as a healthcare provider is to provide education and guidance to help patients make informed decisions about their care. As you explore whether non-stimulant options are the right fit for your daily routine, having clear, open communication is essential. To help guide a thoughtful, personalized conversation at your next doctor’s appointment, I’ve put together a list of key questions to help you get started. Dr. Jo Hughes is a paid consultant compensated by Supernus.

Non-stimulants are noncontrolled prescription medications used to treat the core ADHD symptoms, inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity.

With consistent daily dosing, non-stimulant medications can provide continuous medication exposure over a 24-hour period.

Most non-stimulant medications offer a distinct and targeted approach to help manage daily ADHD symptoms, working gradually over time to improve symptom control.

Every non-stimulant ADHD medication has a different safety profile, so side effects can vary. Having an open conversation with your provider before starting treatment is the best way to ensure your plan fits your needs and daily routine.

Non-stimulants are noncontrolled medications. Talk to your doctor about prescription and refill options, including whether telehealth appointments are appropriate for you.

Qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a convenient once-a-day non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults and kids ages 6 years and older. It was the first non-stimulant ADHD medication approved in over a decade with approximately 3 million prescriptions filled since launch in 2021 (for children 6-17 years old) and 2022 (in adults 18 years and older).

Qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older. Please click here for full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning, and Medication Guide.

Qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Tell your doctor if you or your child have (or if there is a family history of) suicidal thoughts or actions before starting Qelbree. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any new or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

See below for full Important Safety Information.

Finding an ADHD treatment can take time, there isn’t a one-size-fits all approach. Schedule time with your doctor to discuss all your options, including if Qelbree may be a good fit for you.

Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any new or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

You should not take Qelbree if you or your child: Take a medicine for depression called a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) or have stopped taking an MAOI in the past 14 days. Also, you or your child should avoid alosetron, duloxetine, ramelteon, tasimelteon, tizanidine, and theophylline.

Qelbree can increase blood pressure and heart rate. Your or your child’s doctor will monitor these vital signs.

Qelbree may cause manic episodes in patients with bipolar disorder. Tell your doctor if you or your child show any signs of mania.

Do not drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how Qelbree will affect you or your child. Qelbree may cause you or your child to feel sleepy or tired.

The most common side effects of Qelbree in patients 6 to 17 years are sleepiness, not feeling hungry, feeling tired, nausea, vomiting, trouble sleeping, and irritability, and in adults, insomnia, headache, sleepiness, tiredness, nausea, decreased appetite, dry mouth, and constipation. These are not all the possible side effects of Qelbree.

#9383. For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

In this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually showed greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, showed no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups showed improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

In the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them new to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.)

What did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators showed greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

But that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups showed similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

So if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out.   Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

After two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another showed that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

The benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

Imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

For beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

The idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, big-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits.   So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

Using animal characters, educators can help children navigate big feelings with mindfulness and self-compassion.

A study of 38,000 people around the world finds that people who feel connected to nature are more hopeful, purposeful and resilient.

Whether we’ve been trying to improve our exercise, eating, sleep, or happiness, self-reflection is one of the most practical tools we have.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

#9381. Scaling the Wall of Awful

When procrastination stems from anxiety or fear of failure, use this playbook to help your child get unstuck.

Here’s a familiar scenario: Your student with ADHD sits at the kitchen table, supposedly doing homework. Twenty minutes go by, and you check on their status. Nothing has been accomplished.

In these moments, your child is invisibly, involuntarily grappling with the Wall of Awful, a term I coined to describe the emotional barrier people confront when faced with draining and/or daunting tasks (homework is a good example). Before your child can engage in work, they must get past this wall of emotions.

Many parents misinterpret the early warning signs of the Wall. They mistake difficulty starting a task for resistance or defiance. So they double down on being a taskmaster, or, alternatively, they hover and provide too much help. Neither tactic aids their child in the long run.

[Get This Free Download: What Are Your Teen’s Weakest Executive Functions?]

Instead, I recommend talking about the idea of a Wall of Awful that stands between students and certain tasks. Then, when red flags appear, the Wall becomes the problem, not the kid, enabling the parent and child to problem-solve together.

The Wall of Awful can affect anyone, but kids with ADHD are especially susceptible because their weak executive functioning skills make completing tasks harder. These struggles, combined with previous failures or fears of failure, add extra emotional bricks to the Wall.

Here is a quick-start approach that parents can follow to help their student vault the Wall of Awful:

#9380. How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind. But here’s the truth: self-love isn’t something you’re born knowing how to do. It’s something you learn. And like any meaningful practice, it takes time, intention, and a lot of patience.

If you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone. Many of us were never taught how to speak to ourselves with compassion, how to set boundaries that honor our needs, or how to practice everyday self-respect. That’s where this guide comes in—because it’s never too late to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered. It means learning to treat yourself the way you’d treat someone you care deeply about—with gentleness, understanding, and care. Whether you’re struggling with self-worth, navigating difficult emotions, or simply trying to reconnect with the real you, these seven steps offer a foundation for how to practice self-love in real, actionable ways.

From building self-awareness and setting healthy boundaries to practicing forgiveness and celebrating your wins, this guide is here to support your growth. Start small, stay consistent, and trust that loving yourself is not only possible—it’s one of the most empowering things you’ll ever do.

Self-love is exactly how it sounds—it’s a love for yourself and having an interest in your own well-being and happiness. Loving yourself doesn’t mean being self-centered or selfish. It’s about forming a caring relationship with yourself, like getting to know a good friend.

The idea of loving yourself isn’t just a ‘feel-good’ concept—it’s essential for mental health. Research shows that self-compassion is linked to lower stress, reduced anxiety, and even improved physical health. People who actively practice self-love tend to set better boundaries, build stronger relationships, and experience less burnout.

Self-love is important because the relationship you have with yourself sets the tone for how you deal with every aspect of life: your bonds with others, the way you handle challenges, and how you celebrate joys. When you’re kind and understanding toward yourself, you’re better equipped to navigate life’s ups and downs.

But how do you start loving yourself? Where do you even begin? Self-love starts with understanding where you stand right now. Take a look at your current feelings toward your mental health, motivation, and overall well-being. Are you harsh with yourself when things don’t go as planned? Do you forget to celebrate your wins, especially the small ones? These little check-ins can pave the path to walking toward self-love.

Loving yourself isn’t a switch you turn on or off. It’s a practice that takes time, commitment, and, well, practice, to cultivate. For many of us, the idea of loving ourselves feels out of reach. That’s why it’s often helpful to break the concept of self-love down into its distinctive elements — including self-trust, self-compassion, and self-awareness.

This can make it easier to start developing a self-love practice that feels achievable and manageable. So instead of viewing self-love as something you have to win at, try practicing these seven steps.

Self-awareness: Understand your feelings, thoughts, and behaviors.

Self-expression: Be true to who you are in all areas of life.

Self-care: Take care of your body and mind.

Self-trust: Believe in your ability to handle life’s ups and downs.

Self-compassion: Be kind to yourself, especially when times are tough.

Self-respect: Honor your worth by setting healthy boundaries.

Self-acceptance: Embrace who you are, including the parts you don’t find perfect. Remember what we said about perfection?

Sometimes practicing self-love means taking action or establishing boundaries to protect your mental health. Here are a few IRL examples of how you can practice self-love today.

Prioritize rest to recharge: Imagine you’ve had a long week, and instead of squeezing in one more task, you decide to turn off your devices and enjoy a full night’s sleep. Studies have shown that adequate rest improves mood, cognitive function, and emotional resilience​. By honoring your body’s need for recovery, you demonstrate that you value your well-being above productivity.

Say no to unhealthy relationships: Picture being invited to a gathering where you know that certain individuals drain your energy. Choosing to decline isn't selfish; it’s self-preservation. Healthy boundaries are key to having self-respect and healthy relationships. Saying no clears space for connections that truly nourish you​.

Practice forgiveness for yourself: Maybe you’ve made a mistake at work and feel embarrassed. Instead of spiraling into self-criticism, try acknowledging the error, learning from it, and moving on. Self-compassion may help reduce anxiety and create more resilience, helping you recover more effectively from setbacks​. Mistakes are normal, and it’s all about “failing up”.

Create moments of mindfulness amid the chaos: Let’s say your day is hectic, and stress feels overwhelming. This is the moment to pause for a brief grounding exercise (here’s one of our favorites). Maybe you focus on your breath or tune into your surroundings. These types of practice not only calm your nervous system but also remind you of your ability to care for yourself even in small, meaningful ways​.

Treat yourself with the same kindness you show others: When you reflect on a recent accomplishment—big or small—you choose to celebrate it instead of brushing it off. There are huge benefits to recognizing your personal achievements. Giving yourself a pat on the back may help boost self-esteem and even long-term happiness​.

Self-love can feel unfamiliar and challenging to some of us, particularly if we’ve got into a habit of being hard on ourselves. The steps above can help break down the idea of self-love into more manageable elements.

But what practical things can we do to cultivate practices like self-awareness and self-trust? We got you. For each of the self-love steps, we’re sharing tools, techniques and exercises you can use to help get you closer to loving yourself.

Building self-awareness helps cultivate self-love by giving you further insight into what makes you who you are on an emotional level. Begin by tuning into your thoughts and feelings.

What makes you feel happy, sad, or excited? Then, take it a step further. What makes you feel overwhelmed, overjoyed, or anxious? Knowing yourself is the first step to loving yourself.

Practice mindfulness: Try mindfulness practices to stay present and understand your thoughts and feelings better.

Educate yourself: Empower yourself through education by reading books, attending workshops, or engaging in discussions that promote self-awareness, self-compassion, and self-love.

Schedule regular self-check-ins: Reflect on your feelings, goals, and progress. Write them down, and revisit them often.

Tune into yourself through meditation: Spend some quiet time meditating to help declutter your mind and tap into your desires.

Let go of what no longer serves you: Let go of old habits or relationships that no longer contribute to your growth or happiness. We know this practice can be difficult, but removing what no longer brings you joy makes space for the good to come in.

💙 If you want to learn to relate to your thoughts in a healthier way, press play on Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty.

Loving yourself also means giving yourself permission to express your thoughts and feelings both inwardly and outwardly. Express yourself honestly in your day-to-day life. Be true to who you are, whether you’re simply chatting with friends or making big decisions at work.

Engage in creative expression: Whether it's drawing, writing, or any other form of creative expression, allowing your creativity to flow freely can become an act of self-love.

Discover new hobbies: Explore new activities that bring you joy and allow you to express yourself. Have you always wanted to try your hand at a group sport or acting? Now’s the time to try.

Journaling: Write down your thoughts, feelings, and experiences daily, and don’t hold back. Expressing yourself through writing can be cathartic and a helpful step in falling back in love with who you are.

Spend quality time with yourself: Enjoy your own company by doing things that make you happy. There’s a difference between doing something alone and feeling lonely. Embracing solo time and solo outings to the movies, dinner, or even a cooking class can be empowering, and, believe it or not, ridiculously fun!

💙 Journaling can be a great way to process feelings and encourage self-love. Check out our five Calm Journals plus our Feelings Wheel to get you started.

Caring for your body and mind plays a major role in cultivating self-love. Simple acts like mindful eating, exercise, and making time to relax can make a big difference in your overall well-being.

Take breaks when you need them: Remember to rest — even a micro-break can refresh and rejuvenate you. Want to amp up your rest break a notch? Take it outside. Being in nature can naturally calm and refresh your mind and body.

Practice relaxation: Use techniques like deep breathing or yoga to relax your body and focus on your breath.

Nourish your body: Fuel your body with nourishing food that makes you feel good.

Prioritize sleep: Ensure you get enough good-quality sleep—it’s crucial for your well-being.

Connect with your body through movement: Move your body in a way that feels good for you. It could be dancing in your apartment to your favorite album, walking outside, or stretching from the comfort of your bed.

Ask for support when you need it: Reach out for help when you need it. Asking for support is a sign of strength.

💙 Move your body with some Mindful Movement thanks to the Daily Move.

It’s hard to love yourself if you don’t trust yourself. Embracing self-trust is about understanding that you have the ability to make the correct decisions for your life. Even when things don’t go as planned, believing that you can learn and grow from the experience is an important step in building self-trust.

Set realistic expectations: Set achievable goals to build your sense of accomplishment and reinforce the belief you have in yourself to overcome.

Practice patience: Be patient with yourself as you uncover what self-love means to you. Trusting yourself takes time. Let it.

Monitor your negative self-talk: Pay attention to how you talk to yourself. Are you harsh or unforgiving? Do you speak about yourself poorly? Take note of how you speak to yourself and work to make it more positive and encouraging.

Make a list of things you’re proud of: Reflect on your achievements and the things that make you proud. Look back on them when you need a dose of inspiration, and remind yourself and believe that you can make yourself proud again and again.

💙 Check out our 7 Days of Self-Esteem series to build your self-acceptance and boost your inner strength.

Be kind to yourself. Always. Especially when life gets tough. Celebrate your wins, learn from life’s mishaps, and don’t be too hard on yourself when it all doesn’t go as planned. Having compassion for self means you deeply care about your well-being. And feelings of deep care often mean love.

Practice positive affirmations: Craft and repeat positive phrases daily to help drive away those pesky negative thoughts.

Develop a self-forgiveness practice: Forgive yourself for past mistakes or perceived shortcomings. You’re only human. Remember that.

Try a loving-kindness meditation: Practice loving-kindness meditation to cultivate love and kindness toward yourself and others.

Put your hand over your heart and breathe deeply: This simple gesture can bring comfort and a sense of self-compassion.

💙 Try Loving-Kindness Meditation as a guided practice with Tamara Levitt.

Respect yourself by setting boundaries to show yourself—and others—that your desires, wants, and needs matter. When we respect our boundaries and our wants, we’re showing ourselves love by prioritizing our needs.

Seek supportive communities: Surround yourself with supportive, loving, and understanding people who uplift you. The more you’re around people you respect and admire, the more you might begin to respect, admire, and love yourself.

Set boundaries: Give yourself permission to say no to things or people that drain your energy. Setting boundaries and sticking to them is an act of self-love, as it showcases to the world around you that you give yourself what you want and need.

Volunteer: Engage in volunteer work to connect with a sense of purpose and community. Volunteer to walk dogs at a local animal shelter or serve meals at a community kitchen. Giving back brings a deep sense of purpose and gratitude, and a way to give yourself love is to give love to others in need.

Celebrate your progress and success: Celebrate your wins, big or small, as all victories are steps toward growth. You’d cheer for a friend’s achievement, regardless of its size, wouldn’t you? Show yourself the same love and kindness and become your own cheerleader.

Honor your commitments to yourself: When you make a promise to yourself, keep it. Honoring your promises to yourself can help to build self-respect, which, as we’ve learned, enhances self-love by showing yourself that you’re a priority.

💙 Learn even more about self-love with our Relationship with Self series.

Embrace yourself wholeheartedly. Every single inch. Even the parts you’d like to improve upon. You have nothing to gain by being hard on yourself, and everything to gain by being loving and accepting of yourself as you move along on your path in life.

When you accept yourself, you’re declaring the love you have for yourself, regardless of what happens. Think of self-acceptance as a loving embrace.

Learn to laugh with yourself: Embracing a light-hearted approach toward life and how you view yourself can help you meet those challenging moments with more ease and less friction.

Embrace where you are now: Appreciate the present moment. You’re here now. So, be here now and try to enjoy the journey.

Make space for your emotions: Allow yourself to feel your emotions. Emotions are natural, but ignoring them can become detrimental to your well-being.

Drop the comparison: Avoid comparing yourself to others. You’re unique and have your own journey.

Practice gratitude: Cultivate gratitude by acknowledging the qualities you appreciate about yourself and your life. This can shift your focus from what's lacking to what's abundant.

💙 If you’re looking to build a daily gratitude practice, check out the 7 Days of Gratitude.

Morning affirmations: Start your day with one self-loving statement (e.g., "I am enough"). This may reduce stress and boost confidence.

Set small self-care goals: Even five minutes of journaling or stretching may shift your mindset toward self-love.

Mirror work: Look in the mirror and say something kind about yourself. It might feel awkward at first, but it may build self-acceptance.

Limit self-criticism: Notice when you’re being hard on yourself. Pause and reframe it as if you were talking to a friend.

Practice gratitude: Write down three things you appreciate about yourself daily. Gratitude is potentially linked to higher self-worth.

Self-love is essential in relationships because it provides the foundation for healthy, balanced, and meaningful connections. When you love yourself, you develop confidence and emotional stability, which allows you to communicate your needs and feelings openly without fear of judgment. This clarity helps you to form stronger communications and can also reduce misunderstandings. Self-love also empowers you to set and maintain healthy boundaries, ensuring that your relationships are built on mutual respect rather than people-pleasing or overextending yourself. (Learn how to stop being a people pleaser with these 10 tips.)

When you feel secure in your own worth, you can offer love freely without expecting others to validate you, and you’re better equipped to accept care from others because you believe you deserve it. Ultimately, self-love nurtures healthier, more fulfilling connections by allowing you to show up as your best self, while also creating space for others to do the same.

Starting on the path of self-love begins with self-awareness. Notice your thoughts, feelings and actions. Begin to recognize what makes you smile or what makes you feel uneasy. Once you have a better understanding of yourself, you can start taking steps toward treating yourself with more kindness and respect. Remember, it's a journey—there are no deadlines, and you don’t have to rush. And if you ever feel lost, you can always revisit the seven steps to gently reintroduce self-love practices.

If you're struggling to love yourself, start by identifying the thoughts that hold you back. Are you constantly comparing yourself to others? Do you feel unworthy of kindness? Self-love begins with self-awareness. Explore these steps to start loving yourself today:

Shift your internal dialogue: Notice when you're being self-critical and replace it with a more compassionate thought.

Prioritize self-care: Even small acts like deep breathing or a 10-minute walk can reinforce your self-worth.

Surround yourself with positivity: Reduce exposure to toxic relationships or social media comparisons.

Celebrate small wins: Even recognizing personal growth (no matter how small) strengthens self-love.

Struggling with self-love is a common human experience, so you're not alone. Sometimes, past experiences, societal expectations, or harsh self-judgment can create blocks on the path to self-love. It's important to remember that overcoming these hurdles takes time and practice, but with patience and persistence, it can get easier. Engaging in self-compassion practices and seeking support when needed are great steps when you encounter these struggles.

Lack of self-love can show up in different ways. It could be in the form of constant self-criticism, ignoring your own needs, or having difficulty with accepting compliments. It might also appear as feeling undeserving of positive experiences or neglecting self-care. The good news is that recognizing these signs is the first step toward change. Once you see them, you can start taking steps to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Self-love habits are small, daily actions that nurture a loving relationship with yourself. They could be as simple as speaking kindly to yourself, taking breaks when needed, or engaging in activities that make you happy. Other self-love habits include practicing gratitude, spending time in nature, eating nourishing food, and exercising in a way that feels good to your body. The goal is to create habits that make you feel loved, respected, and cared for.

Loving yourself isn’t a switch you flip—it’s a process. If self-love feels out of reach, start small. Acknowledge your feelings without judgment, challenge negative self-talk, and practice one self-kindness daily. Maybe it’s treating yourself with the same patience you’d give a friend, or simply recognizing that you deserve happiness.

One simple trick is to ask yourself, “If my best friend was feeling this way, what would I tell them?”

Often, we extend kindness to others more easily than to ourselves. Flip that perspective inward.

The first step in learning how to love yourself is awareness—tuning into your thoughts, noticing how you speak to yourself, and identifying patterns of self-criticism. Once you're aware of your inner dialogue, you can begin to shift it with self-kindness, small acts of self-care, and daily affirmations. Remember: every loving thought counts.

The meaning of self love is caring for yourself emotionally, physically, and mentally with the same compassion you’d offer someone you love. It means honoring your needs, setting boundaries, and treating yourself with kindness—not just when things are going well, but especially when they aren’t.

#9378. How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:

AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

She argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, important. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

Cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

When working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those important factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

This type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food company, who was responsible for developing new recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so important when working with AI?

CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so important in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

This pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for new information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so important because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

When something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really quickly, sometimes those very important factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

CSE: Francis Bacon once said, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

We need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

One thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

For example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max quickly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”

Only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved?   CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

The first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

When using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more important because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

For AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

So you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

CSE: It’s a great question. I think the new competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

We each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and said to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

There is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

You can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

So I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.
